podcast.title: Formation and Early Cover Gigs (1996)
podcast.body: The band started in 1996 in Colin McDonald's grandmother's basement, playing cover songs, including tracks by Tom Petty, The Beatles, The Tragically Hip, James Brown, and The Black Crowes. They gigged frequently in Antigonish high schools and local bars like Chuggles, Piper's Pub, and Pats Place, sometimes needing permission slips to play underage. "We started in 1996 and my grandmother's basement playing cover songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Name Change to Trouser (2000)
podcast.body: In 2000, after years of playing cover gigs as One-eyed Trouser, the band's manager in Buffalo, New York, suggested shortening their name to "Trouser," believing "eyed" bands were passé. This change coincided with their move from Nova Scotia to Ontario. "So we call our band trouser in 2000."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Jeff Healey's Bar Residency (2001)
podcast.body: Following an opening gig for Jeff Healey in Halifax in Summer 2001, Healey invited the band to be the house band at his new Toronto bar, Healey's, on Bathurst and Queen. The Trews accepted, playing every Thursday throughout Summer and Fall 2001. "He said, look, I'm starting a bar called Healey's. You guys give me my house band every Thursday."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Forced Name Change to The Trews (2002)
podcast.body: Right before the release of their first EP in 2002, which Gordy Johnson produced, the band received a cease and desist letter from an acid jazz band from Mississauga also named "Trouser." Faced with an overnight deadline to rename themselves for the record, Jack Siparek's mother, Jean, suggested "The Trews," explaining it meant "Scottish pants," similar to trousers but distinct from kilts. "Jack's mother, Jean called us and said, you guys should call yourselves the trouser because the trues mean the same thing as trousers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Rock Search Win (2002)
podcast.body: After opening for Big Sugar, a connection facilitated by Larry Wanigas, the band was seen by representatives from 97.7 Hits FM. They were encouraged to enter and subsequently won Rock Search in 2002, which provided them with funds to record at Metalworks studio. "we went and won it in 2002."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Touring with Robert Plant (2005)
podcast.body: The Trews embarked on a full North American tour, "a dozen dates" from Toronto to Victoria, opening for Robert Plant, who was promoting his "Mighty ReArranger" album. Plant was noted for his friendliness, checking out their guitars at their first soundcheck and performing Led Zeppelin songs like "Going to California" and "That's The Way." "we were getting on a bus to tour with the Golden God himself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Japan Trip with Canadian Artists (2008)
podcast.body: In 2008, the band took a trip to Japan to play at the Canadian consulate, sharing a versatile bill at the Oscar Peterson Theatre in Tokyo with artists like Bedouin Soundclash, The Rural Alberta Advantage (then known as Wooden Hands), The Russian Futurists, and Alex Cuba. The venue's inability to accommodate their usual "heavy equipment, loud rock show" prompted their first significant acoustic performance. "we went and played at the consulate with like Bedouin Sound Clash and the band that ended to be the rural Alberta advantage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: "Civilianaires" Recording Departure
podcast.body: The recording of the 2018 album "Civilianaires" marked a change in the band's approach. It was their first record that was not recorded "live off the floor," instead being built up track-by-track in producer Derek Hoffman's basement studio in Toronto. "That was the first time we made a record kind of not live off the floor."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: 25 Years in Career
podcast.body: The band noted they are 25 years into their career, expressing a desire to continue creating music, touring the world, and inspiring each other. They hope their best songs and shows are still ahead, aiming to keep growing and refining their craft for their supportive fanbase. "This is 25 years into our career."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Bruce Springsteen Encore Performance
podcast.body: The Trews performed a 12-minute version of "Twist and Shout" with Bruce Springsteen as an encore after a member was invited by Springsteen during a show. The band ensured they stayed sober enough to perform decently. "we better stay sober enough over the next three hours of his show so we can play twist and shout in the encore decently."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Response
podcast.body: During the COVID-19 pandemic, The Trews adopted various strategies to stay active and connected with fans, including performing online concerts from a couch in Toronto every Friday night, launching a Patreon, songwriting, home demoing, and engaging fans on Instagram and Facebook. They also produced a Zoom-only video for their single "Godspeed Rebel." "we immediately started doing like a lot of online concerts, like a lot of like, I would do sessions from my couch in Toronto, just playing songs every Friday night."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Classic Rock Magazine Support
podcast.body: Classic Rock magazine in the UK has been consistently supportive of The Trews. They nominated the band for a "best new band" award for their second album at the UK Classic Rock Awards, where band members attended alongside figures like Jimmy Page and Steven Tyler. The magazine also reviewed their records and interviewed them regularly. "they nominated us for an award on our second album, like a best new band award at the UK Classic Rock Awards."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Colin McDonald's Illness on Ace Frehley Tour
podcast.body: Before a six-week US tour opening for Ace Frehley at House of Blues venues, Colin McDonald contracted a severe bronchial infection, losing his singing voice for the first three weeks. The audience, largely "die hard Kiss fans," were not typically receptive to new music. He eventually recovered his voice after obtaining antibiotics in America, leading Ace Frehley's famous sound engineer, Nightbob, to jokingly comment that he was "learning how to sing on this tour." "for the first like three weeks at Ace Freyly tour, I couldn't sing. It was a nightmare."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Dave Taylor Becomes Manager
podcast.body: After their second appearance at The Horseshoe, Buffalo, New York promoter Dave Taylor, who promoted several major venues like The Trowel, saw them perform. Impressed, he offered to manage them, helping them secure better shows in Buffalo. "He saw us. He's like, you guys need a manager. I've got clubs. I can get you on some good shows. Let me represent you."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Extensive Touring After Debut Album
podcast.body: The success of "Not Ready To Go" transformed the band's career, leading to relentless touring with "a couple hundred shows a year" in the first few years. They opened for various bands, including Three Days Grace, Evanescence, and Big Sugar, playing in arenas. "suddenly we were getting our first offers to play in arenas opening for bands. And we were on the road all the time, like couple hundred shows a year, easy for those first couple of years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Fan Engagement and Creative Leash
podcast.body: The Trews expressed gratitude for their "really great fans" who allow them a "long leash creatively," following them on diverse musical journeys. The band aims to continue providing exciting, feel-good entertainment that leaves people smiling and singing. "they allow us a long leash creatively. Like they kind of follow us on a lot of our different journeys musically."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Featured in "In Their Own Words" Series
podcast.body: The Trews was featured in the "In Their Own Words" series, which invites multiple band members to share their personal histories. "the Trues, and 5440."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Arena Show Inspiration
podcast.body: A band member's first meaningful arena show was watching The Tragically Hip perform on their "Phantom Power" tour in the late 90s in Halifax. The experience of seeing Gord Downie "own the stage" and the band's delivery left a lasting impact. "watching Downey own the stage the way he did and watched the band deliver on the level that they did. That never left me."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Horseshoe Tavern Breakthrough
podcast.body: During their self-booked national tour, the band secured a "legit gig" at The Horseshoe in Toronto on a new music night, booked by Craig Lasky. Their performance led Lasky to immediately call them back for another booking the next day, prompting the band to frequently return to Toronto. "Craig called us the next day... he's like, when can I book you again?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Larry Wanigas Management
podcast.body: During their residency at Jeff Healey's bar, they caught the attention of legendary manager Larry Wanigas, known for managing k.d. lang and Big Sugar. Wanigas liked the band and introduced them to producer Gordy Johnson, leading to their first album. "Larry Wanigas who is the, you know, legendary manager, he managed Katie Lang and at the time he was managing big sugar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Lifelong Band Connection
podcast.body: Three members, Jack, Johnny, and Collins, describe their connection as lifelong and inspirational, driving them to continually seek new songs and enjoy making music and performing for audiences globally. "the three of us, me and Johnny and Collins formed a connection like years ago. And it feels like that it's a lifelong connection."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Niagara Falls Residency
podcast.body: The band lived for two years in a rented house at 6289 Main Street in Niagara Falls, Ontario, which they described as a "rundown former crack den." This location became crucial to their career, as they established their base there after living across the river in Buffalo at their manager's house, and launched their career from this residence. "We lived there for like two years and we literally got our career off the ground from that house."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Opening for The Rolling Stones
podcast.body: While working on "A Den of Thieves" in Toronto in Summer 2005, rumors surfaced about The Rolling Stones rehearsing for a secret show. Larry Wanigas, unable to get tickets, instead secured The Trews an opening slot at The Phoenix with just 24 hours' notice, contingent on Charlie Watts' health. The band was sworn to secrecy and, upon arriving for soundcheck, found The Rolling Stones already on stage. They earned a photo with the legendary band after their set. "Larry calls... I can't get you tickets, but you can open for them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Original Name: One-eyed Trouser Snake
podcast.body: Before becoming The Trews, Colin McDonald had a punk/grunge band in high school in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia with a friend who shared a love for Monty Python. This earlier band was named One-eyed Trouser Snake, after a song from Monty Python's "Meaning of Life." When the core members (Colin, John Angus, Jack) formed, they adopted a shortened version, "One-eyed Trouser." "me and my buddy from grade nine really liked Monty Python and we called our first band One-eyed trouser snake from that song from Meaning of Life."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Patreon Launch (Pandemic)
podcast.body: At the beginning of the pandemic, The Trews launched a Patreon account. As part of this initiative, they distributed leftover copies of their rare 1997 "One-eyed Trouser EP," which had been stored at Colin McDonald's mother's house, to their "diehard fans." "We launched a Patreon at the beginning of the pandemic and one of the, and we had a bunch of these leftover trouser EPs from my mom's house and we gave them to a bunch of our diehard fans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Self-Booked National Tour
podcast.body: Driven by ambition to break out of Nova Scotia, the band embarked on an audacious self-booked national tour from Antigonish to Vancouver and back. They cold-called numerous venues, often facing rejection, and slept in the back of a van with a bed built over their amps, relying on friends and family for support. "we booked ourselves from anti-genitio to Vancouver and back, sleeping in the back of the van."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Self-Titled Album Magazine Giveaway
podcast.body: For their 2015 self-titled album, Classic Rock magazine packaged the record with every issue, distributing approximately 90,000 copies of it in the UK. This initiative provided significant exposure for the band. "they actually packaged the record with every issue and gave away like 90,000 copies of it in the UK with Classic Rock magazine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: The "Bohemian Rhapsody" Incident
podcast.body: During their tour with Robert Plant, a fan dared The Trews on live radio to perform their old cover of Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" at a sold-out show in Rexall Place, Edmonton. The band delivered a "punky version" that garnered a standing ovation. This angered Robert Plant, who, having known Freddie Mercury, didn't want the past relived. He "accosted" their drummer, Sean, the next day in Calgary, but later issued a public apology by praising Canadian songwriters, including The Trews, at the Saddledome. "we got word that we really ticked Robert Plant off."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: The Bathouse Recording Experience
podcast.body: The band recorded their "Hope and Ruin" album at The Bathouse, The Tragically Hip's studio in Bath, Kingston. This studio is described as an old coach house with a swimming pool, basketball court, grand piano, and living/sleeping quarters upstairs, functioning as a live-work recording space. "It's one of these old-style live work recording studios."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: The Tragically Hip Connection
podcast.body: The Trews opened for The Tragically Hip in 2004 and maintained contact with them, leading to Gord Sinclair producing "Hope and Ruin" at The Bathouse. The Bathouse also served as a "Hip museum," featuring artifacts like the console from "Phantom Power," a painting from "In Between Evolution," and original artwork from "Fully Completely." "getting to work in this like house that's technically a hip museum."

xref.title: Apology and Compliment to The Trews
xref.body: After his initial displeasure regarding The Trews' "Bohemian Rhapsody" cover, Robert Plant later offered a subtle apology during a show in Calgary at the Saddledome. He publicly acknowledged Canada's rich songwriting history, mentioning Neil Young, Joni Mitchell, and Leonard Cohen, and significantly, included "the trues" in this esteemed list. "Canada has always had such a rich history of songwriting and with Neil Young and Joni Mitchell and Leonard Cohen and the trues. And I took that as his his apology for telling us."

xref.title: Disapproval of "Bohemian Rhapsody" Cover
xref.body: Robert Plant expressed strong disapproval when The Trews performed a "punky version" of Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" during their shared tour, especially after it earned them a standing ovation. He conveyed his feelings by stating he knew Freddie Mercury and felt it was inappropriate to "relive the past," even directly accosting their drummer Sean about it. "He didn't want us doing that anymore... he told us it was because he knew Freddie and we're not here to relive the past."

"I started playing in like not serious like kind of punk and grunge bands in high school with my friends."

This collaboration stemmed from a long-standing relationship, including The Trews opening for The Hip in 2004. "Gord offered us some days to come up to Bath and write and record and just jam and hang out and see how it feels."

xref.title: Impromptu Collaboration with The Trews

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Interaction with The Trews
xref.body: Despite his reputation for not socializing before shows, Bruce Springsteen drove his golf cart directly up to The Trews and engaged them in a brief, energetic conversation, asking where they were from. This direct interaction left a strong impression on the band. "He just came right up and he's like, how you doing? We're like, oh, good man. Good, Bruce Springsteen. We're good."

"Jack's mother, Jean called us and said, you guys should call yourselves the trouser because the trues mean the same thing as trousers."

"we wanted to work with somebody who worked with Nirvana."

xref.title: Shared Bill in Japan (as Wooden Hands)
xref.body: Before becoming The Rural Alberta Advantage, the band performed under the name "Wooden Hands" on a "really versatile bill" at the Oscar Peterson Theatre in Tokyo, Japan. They shared the stage with The Trews, Bedouin Soundclash, The Russian Futurists, and Alex Cuba as part of a trip to play at the Canadian consulate. "the band that ended up being the rural Alberta advantage. I think they recalled something else back then wooden hands or something that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

xref.title: Shared Bill with Bruce Springsteen
xref.body: Tom Cochrane performed on the same bill as The Trews and Bruce Springsteen at Magnetic Hill in Moncton, New Brunswick, on a day described as "a beautiful day" in late August. "it was us in Tom Cochrane and Bruce Springsteen and it's got a beautiful day and late August."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

xref.title: Supportive Crew
xref.body: The crew working for Ace Frehley during his US tour with The Trews were noted for being "super accommodating and really sweet." This support was particularly appreciated by Colin McDonald, who was suffering from a severe bronchial infection at the time. "their crew was always really cool with us. They were super accommodating and really sweet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

xref.title: The Bathhouse Recording Studio
xref.body: The Tragically Hip owns and operates its own recording studio, known as The Bathhouse, located outside of Kingston. This studio has served as a recording location for numerous other artists, including Blue Rodeo, Big Rec, Sarah Harmer, Blackie and the Rodeo Kings, Hayden, The Sadies, Kathleen Edwards, The Trews, and The Mahones. "The hip has their own recording studio outside of Kingston called the Bathhouse. Blue Rodeo, Big Rec, Sarah Harmer, Blacky and the Rodeo Kings, Hayden, the Sadies, Kathleen Edwards, the Trues, the Mahones and dozens of others have used the place."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Tragically Hip: A Retrospective

xref.title: The Bathouse Studio
xref.body: The Tragically Hip's studio in Bath, Kingston, known as The Bathouse, is described as an old coach house equipped with various amenities like a swimming pool, basketball court, grand piano, and living quarters, making it a live-work recording environment. The Trews recorded their album "Hope and Ruin" there. "It's one of these old-style live work recording studios."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: The Trews Opened for Him (Moncton)
xref.body: The Trews had the opportunity to open for Bruce Springsteen at Magnetic Hill in Moncton, New Brunswick, after asking if he was looking for an opening act. The concert also featured Tom Cochrane and took place on a "beautiful day" in late August. "We opened form down in in Monkton, uh, Monkton, New Brunswick, uh, Magnetic Hill."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tour with The Trews
xref.body: Robert Plant embarked on a full North American tour with The Trews opening for him, spanning from Toronto to Victoria, including about a dozen dates in arenas. He was promoting his "Mighty ReArranger" album, often referred to as "strange sensation." "that was a whole tour. We did, we went from like Toronto to Victoria doing like the rinks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

xref.title: Toured with The Trews
xref.body: Three Days Grace toured with The Trews, who often "piggybacked" on larger tours in the years following their debut album's success. "We would do a, a run with three days grace."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Toured with The Trews
xref.body: Evanescence toured with The Trews, who were frequently on the road, performing hundreds of shows a year and opening for various bands after their debut album. "a run with, have an essence."

xref.title: Toured with The Trews
xref.body: Big Sugar toured with The Trews, who often opened for them. The connection with Big Sugar's manager, Larry Wanigas, also led to The Trews meeting producer Gordy Johnson. "a run with big sugar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: US Tour with The Trews
xref.body: Ace Frehley toured the United States with The Trews as his opening act for a six-week trek, performing in House of Blues venues across the country. The audiences for these shows were predominantly "die-hard Kiss fans" who were not necessarily open to new music. "We ended up doing like six week trek, opening for Ace Freyly at House of Blues all over America."
